description: Coal seam fields: one deposit is one minable seam field, tens of km across (300-6,000 km2: a Jharia, Gillette or Witbank-sized field; not a mine block, not a whole basin) holding a stack of seams; fields adjoin in a basin. Peat mires preserved where accommodation kept pace with peat production, after land plants; rank from burial heating.

source.note: peat-mire facies from the strata log (Bohacs & Suter 1997)

driver.note: accommodation roughly matching peat production; excess drowns mires (Bohacs & Suter 1997); numbers are design

notes: DEFINITION (Ben, decisions log 2026-09-29, "OK; define coal as seams"): one deposit is ONE MINABLE SEAM FIELD, a contiguous area of coal-bearing strata with minable seams, tens of km across: field area 300 / 1,000 / 6,000 km2 (P90 / P50 / P10; about 20-90 km across; the P10 was 3,000 km2 until Ben's answer of 2026-10-02,

: several real named fields are larger, Gillette 4,150, Witbank 5,680, Highveld 7,000 km2). Comparable named units (stage 2 WP-9/10, 2026-10-02, read in the sources): the Gillette coalfield study area 4,152 km2 (1,026,000 acres; resource area 3,610 km2; USGS PP 1625-A chap. PG); a Pennsylvania anthracite field (four fields in 484 mi2 = 1,254 km2, mean 313 km2; Averitt 1975); South Africa's 19 coalfields over about 97,000 km2 (mean 5,100 km2; Witbank 5,680, Highveld 7,000, Waterberg 3,600, South Rand 600; Hancox & Gotz 2014); India's ~150 coalfields and lignite occurrences over 34,700 km2 (mean ~230 km2; USGS OFR 2011-1296). Named fields therefore run from a few hundred km2 (Gondwana, anthracite) to several thousand (South Africa, Powder River); the P10 3,000 km2 lies below the larger ones. Not a mine-sized measured block (Circular 891: measured radius 0.4 km, indicated 1.2 km) and not a whole basin or coal province (Circular 891 glossary, printed p. 8: a coal FIELD is 'a discrete area underlain by strata containing one or more coal beds'; a region holds fields, a province holds regions). ESTIMATE, not a USGS figure: no source counts minable seam fields with a common rule.

DENSITY 4 / 14 / 40 per 100,000 km2 of permissive coal-bearing tract (P90 / P50 / P10; density_basis 'estimate', so the survivor formula uses the P50, 14). Derivation redone from the sources in stage 2 (WP-9/10, 2026-10-02; first written 2026-09-29), density = named fields / coal-bearing area x 1e5, each count the naming of one survey: Powder River, 12 coal fields named in USGS PP 1625-A chaps. PS and PN (text and reference titles) over the Fort Union Formation's 22,000 mi2 = 56,980 km2 (formation extent; the Wyodak-Anderson resource area is 21,911 km2): 21.1 (the 2026-09-29 count of 6-9 gave 10.5-15.8). Sydney Basin onshore, five coalfields named by the Coalfield Geology Council of NSW over about 36,000 km2 (Bioregional Assessments context statement 1.1; the basin, so non-coal strata included): 13.9. Appalachian basin, 23 coal fields named in USGS PP 1708 chap. D.1 over about 173,500 km2 (the sum of the states' coal-bearing areas in Averitt 1975 Table 1, eastern Kentucky estimated): 13.3. South Africa, 19 coalfields over their own 97,000 km2: 19.6 (fields tile that area, so an upper case). Illinois Basin, coal-bearing rocks 36,800 mi2 in Illinois, 6,500 in Indiana and 6,400 in western Kentucky = 49,700 mi2 = 128,723 km2 (Hatch & Affolter 2002, PP 1625-D, p. A1; the 36,800 mi2 used on 2026-09-29 is Illinois alone), which USGS treats as one region and the state surveys as two named fields and Indiana's part: 2.3. India, ~150 entries over 3.29 million km2 of land: 4.6, a floor (land is not a tract). The median of the five basins with a coal-bearing denominator (2.3, 13.3, 13.9, 19.6, 21.1) is 13.9: the P50 14 stands. The P90 4 and P10 40 are judgement (Illinois and India below 5; the Powder River count over its 21,911 km2 resource area gives 55); the engine does not use them. Upper Silesia's 'three coal areas' (2026-09-29) is in no source read: the basin is 5,600 km2 with 120 documented deposits over 3,295 km2 (Smolinski et al. 2014), a mine-scale unit. Geometric check, 1e5 x f / A with f the share of the tract the fields cover and A the mean field area: the coded area distribution has a mean of about 1,500 km2, so P50 14 is f about 0.21. Not found in any source read: Bowen Basin coalfield counts (Geoscience Australia gives the basin as about 160,000 km2, half under the Surat Basin), Chinese and European coalfield counts.

SOURCES (read in stage 2, WP-9/10, 2026-10-02): USGS Circular 891 (Wood et al. 1983) glossary (printed p. 8), Table 2 and Table 3 (printed p. 24); Averitt 1975, USGS Bulletin 1412 (coal-bearing rocks 458,600 mi2 = 13 % of the US, Table 1 by state; Mammoth zone 3,300 mi2 originally, 484 mi2 in four anthracite fields); USGS PP 1625-A chap. PG (Gillette coalfield, 1,026,000 acres), chap. PS (Flores & Bader; Fort Union 22,000 mi2) and chap. PN (Wyodak-Anderson, 5,414,000 acres); USGS PP 1625-D (Hatch & Affolter 2002; Illinois Basin coal-bearing areas by state); USGS PP 1708 chap. D.1 (Appalachian coal fields); USGS OFR 2011-1296 (Trippi & Tewalt 2011; Table 1 names India's coalfields, no per-field areas; 34.7 thousand km2 of coalfield, CFRI 1993); Bioregional Assessments Programme, Sydney Basin context statement (36,000 km2 onshore, five coalfields); Jeffrey 2005, SAIMM J. 105(2) (19 coalfields, Table I seams); Hancox & Gotz 2014, Int. J. Coal Geol. 132 (coalfield areas); Smolinski et al. 2014 (Upper Silesia). The per-field areas of Jharia, Raniganj, North Karanpura and Singrauli quoted on 2026-09-29 came from Wikipedia and are not in OFR 2011-1296; they are no longer used.

TONNAGE 3,870 / 23,000 / 193,000 Mt (P90 / P50 / P10; 3,800 / 19,800 / 115,000 with the old P10 area of 3,000 km2) = field area x CUMULATIVE minable seam thickness x 1.32 t/m3 (rebased 2026-09-29 when a field became a stack of seams). Area 300 / 1,000 / 6,000 km2; cumulative thickness (the sum of a field's seams, not one bed) 5 / 14 / 60 m, a judgement from the coalfields the stacking research tabulated (cumulative coal, m: Illinois Basin 4.6-14, Appalachian Allegheny Group 6-12, Highveld 6-19, Illawarra 12-20, Witbank 8-32, Powder River net 30-46 in one merged zone, Jharia ~100, Upper Silesia paralic ~137; checked in stage 2: Witbank 7.5-32 and Highveld 3.5-18 (sums of SAIMM Table I seam ranges), Illawarra 11-22 (Bulli, Wongawilli, Balgownie and Tongarra averages, Bioregional Assessments), Powder River mean net coal 17.5-21.2 m over the resource areas (the 30-46 m is the 100-150 ft class of Table PG-2), Upper Silesia ~137 m is all 110 paralic seams of 1-1.5 m, not a minable sum (Smolinski et al. 2014); the Illinois, Allegheny and Jharia sums are not stated in any source read; USGS PP 1625-D, PP 1625-A chap. PS, PP 1708-D1, SAIMM J. 105(2) Table I, Bioregional Assessments, NMET Jharia proposal; several are the research's own arithmetic, see the STATUS entry), the two treated as independent split lognormals and combined by simulation (P10 / P50 / P90 of the product 3,813 / 19,774 / 114,611 Mt). About 19.8 Mt per km2 at the median (19,800 Mt over 1,000 km2; the '15' written on 2026-09-29 was the median thickness in metres); Earth: the Powder River's Wyodak-Anderson about 23 Mt per km2 (550,000 million short tons over 21,911 km2, PP 1625-A chap. PN), Illinois about 1.4-1.9 (a basin-wide average). An ESTIMATE, not a USGS distribution. Was 540 / 2,500 / 10,000 Mt with ONE bed's thickness (Circular 891's classes 0.71 / 2.13 / 4.27 m), which a stack of seams outgrows. COE's vein amount follows the site's tonnage QUANTILE in this distribution, so rebasing it does not change amounts.

GEOMETRY: aspect (1, 5.15e-4, 1.5): the field is a cylinder with x : z = 1 : 1.5 whose thickness 2b is the cumulative seam thickness, so at 19,800 Mt the semi-axes are 14.6 km x 7.5 m x 21.9 km, a 1,000 km2 field with 15 m of coal (29 x 44 km across; 49 x 73 blocks semi-axis at 300 m per block). The engine scales all three axes by the cube root of volume, so the tonnage P90 / P50 / P10 give 337 km2 x 8.7 m, 1,105 km2 x 15.8 m and 4,560 km2 x 32 m (before the 2026-10-02 P10 change: 3,230 km2 x 27 m at the P10). The drawn footprint's P10 (4,560 km2) stays below the sourced area P10 (6,000 km2) because the engine spreads a larger tonnage over thickness as well as area. size_mult_h 1: the body IS the field. size_mult_v 20: a metre of coal is a block.

STACK (geometry.stack; Ben, decisions log 2026-09-29, adjoining + stacked): the field holds several parallel seams, written as one body per seam (role ore, consecutive ids, same footprint, yaw and dip), the field's tonnage split across them by thickness (share_sigma 0.7: seam thickness P10-P90 about a factor 7, the research's 0.8-6 m). Count n = round(S / 25 m) clamped to 1-40 and to cumulative thickness / 0.7 m (Circular 891: 28 in, the bituminous reserve-base minimum; no thinner seam is minable), where S is the coal measures the recorded history laid down under the site while its cell was coal-forming: sum over frames of F x deposition x dt, F the cell's favourability (deposition_rate_m_myr and coal_facies are the history's own fields). 25 m of measures per seam and 40 seams at most from the tabulated coalfields (measures per seam: Appalachian Allegheny ~15, Illinois ~11-29, Ruhr 12 for all coals and ~60 for the economic ones, Upper Silesia ~35, Jharia ~19, Highveld 16-60, Illawarra ~27; mineable seams per section: Illinois 40+ named and 20 of minable thickness (Averitt 1975 p. 8; the '75 named' of 2026-09-29 is in no source read), Llewellyn up to 40, Donets 30-40 workable, Highveld 5, Sydney 4 principal units; Heckel 1986 and Rasbury et al. 1998 cyclothems of 160,000-400,000 yr, about one minable seam per two to four cycles). Gaps between seams: gap_sigma 0.6 (a factor 5 P10-P90, the research's 12-60 m). spacing_mult_v 6 enlarges the gaps in blocks as size_mult_v does thickness (25 m is 1.25 blocks at 20 m per block, too tight to tell seams apart; now 7.5 blocks). The top seam lies half the measures above the ledger's centre depth; erosion drops seams above the ground from the top and clips the one crossing it; the site's tonnage is what is left.

ADJOINING (Ben, decisions log 2026-09-29): sizing.clustering model 'adjoining' and min_separation_m 0: fields fill a basin's minable area, touching but never overlapping in plan (each placed at random in the tract, largest first, where its ellipse crosses none already placed; the yaw is drawn at placement). The camp spacing and Gaussian clustering of the first version (100 / 40 km) are gone for coal.

Density of coal in the ground 1.32 t/m3 for bituminous coal: USGS Circular 891 (Wood et al. 1983), Table 2 p. 22 (1,800 short tons per acre-foot; anthracite 1.47, subbituminous 1.30, lignite 1.29 in data/usgs/coal.json).

PLACEHOLDERS that remain: formation_depth_m 800. The assessment depth is USGS Circular 891's: coal deeper than 6,000 ft (1,800 m) is excluded from resources (printed p. 24, Table 3 p. 24). Design values: the curves, dip, size_mult_v 20.

Rank from Lopatin TTI of the coal layer: TTI 75 <-> Ro ~ 1.1 % (Waples' correspondence as tabulated by the Kansas Geological Survey, non-USGS; the high-volatile bituminous limit). The lignite, subbituminous and low-volatile bounds are PLACEHOLDERS (no USGS table of reflectance by rank was found).
